To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) glycogen is rapidly lost from isolated parenchymal rat liver cells when incubated with high concentrations of glucose; (2) the loss of glycogen is inhibited by glycerol or by fructose but not by insulin; (3) the addition of glyceraldehyde to glucose and glycerol results in more glycogen synthesis; (4) xylitol is more effective than fructose in stimulating glycogen synthesis in cells incubated with glycolysis inhibitors and
glycogen levels in liver are controlled by substrate supply, and that the main effect on glycogen levels of insulin in vivo may be a reduction in the flow of free fatty acid to the liver.

(1) the addition of glycerolphosphate to isolated hepatocytes from rats fed a high carbohydrate diet prevents the breakdown of glycogen; (2) the addition of glucose to isolated hepatocytes causes rapid glycogen breakdown; (3) the addition of oleate to hepatocytes causes rapid breakdown of glycogen.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the synthesis and degradation of glycogen in isolated rat hepatocytes.
the regulation of glycogen synthesis and breakdown in the liver and the role of fatty acids and glycerol in these processes.
the role of glycolytic intermediates in the regulation of glycogen metabolism in liver.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glycogen levels in liver cells in vivo can be controlled by the rate of flow of fatty acids to the cell.
the control of liver glycogen levels is dependent upon the relative concentrations of the various substrates available to the liver.
glycogen is not a simple storage material, but a dynamic metabolic pool which is under strict control of a number of different factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the liver is a very important organ for glycogen metabolism.

the glycogen levels in the hepatocytes of the liver are dependent on the availability of substrates for glycolysis and glycogen synthesis, and that the availability of the substrates is controlled by the hormonal environment.
the glycogen levels of isolated liver cells from fed animals can be maintained by the addition of glyceride glycerol to the incubation medium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver can use glycerol for glycogen storage.
the main effect is the effect of the main effect.
the main effect that insulin has on liver glycogen is to decrease fatty acid delivery to the liver, and this decreases glycogenolysis.
